opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that those are two pretty different problems that we sometimes blur together because they both produce something that *looks* like a building.

Visual generation is fundamentally about plausibility. When a model generates an image or even a 3D scene, the bar is, "Does this look right to a human observer?" And models have gotten incredibly good at that, because the training signal is basically all the pixels in the world. But looking right and *being* right are not the same thing. You can generate a gorgeous cantilevered house that would fall over the moment you built it, and the model has no idea, because nothing in its objective ever asked whether the load paths make sense.

Architectural design, the real kind, is a constraint satisfaction problem layered on top of an aesthetic problem. You've got structural loads, materials, codes, egress, HVAC, cost. Those constraints are hard, not soft. You can't be 90% compliant with a fire code.

So could one model do both? I think eventually something like that is plausible, but probably not as a single end-to-end pixel model. The more likely path is a model with a genuinely 3D, structured internal representation of the world: geometry, materials, physical properties. That's a big part of why I'm excited about spatial intelligence more broadly. Once your representation is actually three-dimensional and physically grounded, rather than just a projection onto a 2D image, you can start hooking it into verifiers, simulators, and solvers that check the physics.

I'd think of it as a generative model that proposes designs in a rich 3D space, paired with tools that tell it, "This beam is overstressed," or "This stair violates code," and then iterating. That's kind of how human architects work too. Nobody designs a skyscraper in one forward pass. There's a creative loop and an engineering loop that keep talking to each other.

So I'm optimistic, but I think the key unlock isn't just scaling up image models. It's getting the representation right, so the model is reasoning about the world itself and not just pictures of it.

r001.rationale: The response says visual models lack objectives that check load paths, but it does not ask whether they could implicitly learn physical forces without force-prediction training.

r002.rationale: It says scaling image models alone is not the key unlock, but does not identify increased scale as a setting where other large models have shown emergent capabilities.

r003.rationale: It considers whether one model could handle generation and reliable design, but does not frame transfer of emergent capabilities across modalities and tasks as an open question.

fable-5.1.text:
I think those are actually two quite different problems that happen to share a surface, and the surface is images. Visual generation is about producing something that looks plausible. Architectural design that's physically reliable is about producing something that is correct, where the ground truth is physics, codes, loads, materials, and the cost of being wrong is a building that doesn't stand up. So the question I'd ask is less "can one model do both" and more "what is the model actually being optimized for, and does the training signal ever touch the thing you care about."

Right now, generative models of images and video are trained on appearance. They learn a staggering amount about the world as a side effect, including a lot of implicit geometry and a kind of folk physics, because you can't predict pixels well without it. That's genuinely impressive, and it's why you can prompt one of these models for a cantilevered house over a cliff and get something that looks like a photo from a design magazine. But "looks like it would stand" and "would stand" are different objectives, and the model has only ever been rewarded for the first one. I've spent a lot of time on 3D and on trying to get networks to produce representations that are consistent in a geometric sense, and even that, which is a much weaker requirement than structural validity, is hard to get purely from appearance supervision.

So my honest view is that a single model will plausibly handle both, but not by getting the diffusion model to be a structural engineer. It'll be because the model becomes more of an orchestrator. It generates a design, it emits or operates on an explicit representation, something like a parametric or CAD-style model rather than pixels, and then it calls into tools that are actually grounded in physics, finite element solvers, code checkers, cost estimators, and takes the feedback. That loop is where reliability comes from. The generative part gives you the creative breadth and the fast iteration on what a space could feel like. The verification part gives you the guarantees. And I think the interesting research question is the interface between them, how you make the generative model fluent in a representation that a verifier can actually consume, and how you get verifier feedback to flow back into the generative process in a way that's more than just rejection sampling.

There's also a dataset issue that I think people underrate. There are billions of images of buildings. There are not billions of buildings paired with their structural calculations, their failure modes, and the reasons certain decisions were made. The thing you'd want the model to learn, the mapping from form to physical consequence, is barely represented in what's on the internet. You can get some of it from simulation, and I'm pretty optimistic about simulation as a source of that kind of supervision, but you have to be deliberate about it. It won't fall out of scaling an image model.

So I'd put it this way. One model handling both is the right long-term picture, but the model that does it won't look like today's image generators with more parameters. It'll be a system that knows when it's in "imagine" mode and when it's in "verify" mode, and the real engineering is in making sure it never confuses the two when someone's life depends on the answer.

r001.rationale: The response says appearance-trained models can acquire implicit geometry and “folk physics,” but it does not ask whether they can learn physical forces without being trained to predict them.

r002.rationale: It says the desired system will differ from today’s image generators, but does not identify increased scale as a setting where emergent capabilities have appeared in other large models.

r003.rationale: It presents the interface between generation and verification as a research question, but does not treat transfer of emergent capabilities across modalities and tasks as an open question.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an exciting possibility, but there’s a pretty big gap between generating something that looks like a plausible building and designing a building that actually stands up. An image can be visually convincing while hiding all sorts of inconsistencies. In architectural design, those inconsistencies matter—you have materials, loads, geometry, and constraints that have to be satisfied together.

So I wouldn’t assume that getting better at visual generation automatically gives you physically reliable design. You’d want some way to check the model’s proposals against those constraints, perhaps using simulation or engineering tools, and then let it iterate based on that feedback.

Could one model ultimately coordinate all of that? Sure, I think that’s plausible. But I’d distinguish between one model being the interface to that process and one model internally knowing enough that you can trust everything it produces. The first seems much easier to imagine than the second.

r002.rationale: It does not mention increased scale or emergent capabilities appearing in other large models.

r003.rationale: It considers whether one model could coordinate visual generation and reliable design, but does not frame transfer of emergent capabilities to other modalities and tasks as an open question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are related capabilities, but there’s a pretty big gap between generating something that looks like a plausible building and designing something that actually stands up. A model can produce a beautiful image without having a consistent account of the geometry, the materials, or how loads move through the structure.

So I’m open to one model eventually doing both, but I wouldn’t assume that getting better at visual generation automatically gives you physical reliability. You’d want it to work with explicit constraints, use simulation and engineering tools, and check its proposals. The interesting question is whether the model can move between imagining a design and testing it—and revise the design when those tests fail. That’s a much stronger capability than making a convincing picture.

r001.rationale: It discusses physical reliability and recommends explicit constraints, simulation, and checking, but does not ask whether a model can implicitly learn forces without being trained to predict them.

r002.rationale: It does not mention increased scale or emergent capabilities in other large models.
